name: Kere-Bavi: Mapping the Hidden Waterscapes of Cubbon Park
description:
Join us for a field walk through Cubbon Park and Sampangi Lake, followed by a hands-on counter-mapping zine workshop exploring Bengaluru’s hidden water stories. Led by Biome Environmental Trust and Paani Earth Foundation, the walk will invite participants to observe recharge wells, stormwater drains, built surfaces and changing landscapes, uncovering the histories and ecologies that often remain unseen.


Back at the Museum, participants will translate their observations into a collective field zine using sketches, surface imprints, found materials and recycled handmade paper, creating alternative maps that bring together the visible and invisible layers of the city’s water systems.

Presented as an extension of Deccan Waters, an exhibition by the Living Waters Museum, the workshop explores the relationship between water, urbanisation, ecology and cultural memory, encouraging participants to look at Bengaluru’s everyday landscapes through the lens of water.

name: A Closer Look: The Painted Imaginaries of Fiza Khatri
description:
Brick Library, 2026, 59 x 85 inches, oil on canvas. Courtesy the artist and Jhaveri Contemporary.
In The Great Rebuild! recently shown with Jhaveri Contemporary, artist Fiza Khatri's invite us into the playful world of children. We see them inhabiting the shifting terrain between play and reality, transforming everyday objects into vessels for imagined journeys. Their irreverent world-building mimics the war and destruction they see around them, building shelters from sofa cushions, playing doctor-patient. Here, building and unbuilding become gestures of possibility, and play becomes a way of rehearsing, reflecting upon and remaking the conditions of existence.

In this edition of A Closer Look, Khatri takes us through the making of this series, and, more broadly, the evolving concerns that animate their practice at large. Across their practice, painting is as much an observational exercise as it is an exercise in imagination. Their paintings bring human and non-human figures into intimate, often unpredictable relationships, allowing bodies, objects, plants and landscapes to coexist without settling into fixed hierarchies or identities. Boundaries between the animate and inanimate, the familiar and the fantastical, tenderness and violence, the sacred and the everyday begin to dissolve. Their paintings invite a kind of looking that is also a form of sensing, or feeling, drawing from the material tactility of the medium itself: the weight, softness, texture or unruliness of things. Meaning is not always immediately legible; it takes shape through the layers that make their work, the stories they contain and the beauty they offer that is so deeply tied to the complexities of lived experience. Moving backwards through their practice, this talk considers how Khatri’s paintings create spaces in which different forms of life, knowledge and feeling might meet, and how painting can become a means of imagining ways of being together otherwise.

This programme at MAP is part of A Closer Look, a monthly series of research-focused talks by artists, curators and art historians focusing on visual cultures of South Asia

name: On Seeing and Being Seen
description:
Joseph Lawrence
In documenting dissent, what is framed, and what is left out? Beyond the image itself, how might we understand the circumstances in which it is produced and circulated? This conversation explores the role of images in moments of resistance considering how they can foster solidarity, while also becoming instruments of State surveillance. As images travel across platforms and contexts, our relationships with them shift, bringing questions of authorship, agency, and ethical representation to the fore. 

This event  is part of Art is Life: Online as part of our annual festival Art is Life.

name: Make At MAP
description: Have you spotted the bougainvillea in bloom at MAP yet? Come join us beneath Martin OC’s painted bougainvillea, get inspired by its beautiful colours, make a few paper flowers of your own and take them home.

name: Training Programme in Principles of Conservation of Photographic Materials: Building practical skills to preserve photographic heritage
description:
This training programme combines the principles of conservation of photographic materials with practical training in preventive care. Organised by the Museum of Art and Photography (MAP) with support from Tata Trusts, it builds on MAP’s 2025 course on conservation of photographs. Intended as an intensive,  hands-on programme, it hopes to bring together conservators, archivists, and custodians of historic photograph collections, with teaching imparted by specialists in the relevant fields.

Over two months, participants will follow a practice-based, structured training format that familiarises them with the history and materiality of photographic materials, followed by intensive identification and documentation practice, and practical conservation strategies. The participants are expected to deepen their knowledge of photographic materials, accurately identify signs of deterioration, apply preventive conservation techniques and develop conservation treatment plans in consultation with photographs conservation experts. 

It will cover:

History and evolution of photographic processes

Rediscovering historic photographic processes

Identification of photographic materials

Deterioration of photographic materials

Condition assessment, documentation, and archiving

Elements of digitisation

Preventive conservation: handling, display, and storage

Disaster management

Why

Photography is  one of the most prolific  forms  of visual art .  Its significance extends beyond aesthetic expression. Photographs serve as historical evidence, artistic interpretations, and material artefacts that preserve traces of particular people, places, events, and societies. Photographic collections are therefore valuable resources for understanding modern history.  However, given the  diversity in the material composition and the sensitive nature of photographs, the passage of time, inadequate storage, and inappropriate handling put photographic collections in libraries, archives, and other institutions at great risk. Caring for photographs requires specialised knowledge, but opportunities to learn these skills in India remain limited.

The two-months-long training programme in principles of conservation of photographic materials is designed to impart these skills and develop critical thinking on conservation of photographs.

Who should apply?

The programme is designed for practicing art conservators who work with photographic collections, as well as custodians of photographic collections from libraries, archives, museums, and other institutions. 

Financial Assistance

There is no fee charged for this course. Modest merit-cum-means scholarships will be available to selected candidates. 

Participants will be requested to arrange their own accommodation, travel, and meals.

How to apply

To apply, complete the online application form by 10th December 2026. 

For questions about the programme, contact rini.hazel@map-india.org

name: Turtle Walker
description:
Umeed Mistry
In the late 1970s, Satish Bhaskar embarked on an epic journey along India's coastline and the spectacular Andaman and Nicobar Islands, where he uncovered the vital nesting beaches of sea turtles. During his death-defying quest, he unravels mysteries surrounding these enigmatic ocean creatures – and sets out to save them from extinction. After a devastating tsunami strikes in 2004, Bhaskar grapples with a pressing question: What happens to sea turtles when their nesting beaches disappear?

The screening will be followed by an online conversation with the director, Taira Malaney. 

This event is in conjunction with the ongoing exhibition, Beneath the Turning Sky.

name: Seeing as an Act of Becoming
description:
Act II, Lakshmi Nivas Collective, 2026, Reclaimed iron, patina on brass cast, 42 x 40 x 40 inches, Edition: unique,
Immortality of Soil, Gallery Maskara
What is revealed when artistic modes of inquiry are applied to local agrarian landscapes? What forms of knowledge, relation, and belonging endure in our encounters with the land, and what recedes from view? In this conversation, we revisit questions of our entanglement with the natural world, asking what material can reveal about ecological and embodied ways of knowing. What are the limits of an anthropocentric worldview, and what alternative ways of seeing, sensing, and relating might emerge in its place?

Join Namrata Neog and Sunoj D from Lakshmi Nivas Collective in conversation with Breanne Coelho from the MAP Team, as they reflect and extend on the ideas and themes from their most recent exhibition, Immortality of Soil at Gallery Maskara, as well as MAP's ongoing exhibition, Beneath the Turning Sky.

This talk is part of Shared Futures, a series spotlighting the work and practices of select artists from the exhibition and beyond, providing audiences a glimpse into their creative method through diverse formats. Through these encounters, we aim to ask what the arts offer in turbulent times. How can we pave new pathways to forge ways of thinking, being and solidarity?

name: Image politic/s
description:
Bani Abidi, Trembling hands, 2024, chalk pastel on paper
Evidentiary tools such as the analogue camera, the canvas and now digital technologies, have long interrogated the obduracy of facts and the singularity of truth in the hands of artists. Observing political events as they unfold in the present, this panel dialogues with practitioners who have long scrutinised cataclysmic moments of the 20th/21st century, manifesting them through fragments and tableaus that re-frame both real and poetic frictions between events and their representations. At this post-digital moment, how might we infer moments in history and their effects on communities through multiple aesthetic registers? What might be discovered at the interpretive site of art-making that could question the paradoxical status of the image, reconstituted as a meld of evidence, artifact and departure? 

This event  is part of Art is Life: Online as part of our annual festival Art is Life.

name: On Conflict, Co-Existence and Development
description:
Conflict and Co-Existence brings together five short documentary films - Mahadwar (The Great Corridor), Pakdam Pakdai, Manaveeyam, Through the Dappled Light and Samayada Harivu (Flow of Time) - that explore the evolving relationship between people, communities and the urban spaces they inhabit. Spanning cities across India, the films examine how development, urbanisation, shifting landscapes and questions of access shape everyday lives. 

Through stories of changing neighbourhoods, children reclaiming public spaces through play, informal workers finding belonging in the city, and communities negotiating their relationship with shared natural resources, the screenings reflect on the tensions and possibilities of urban life. Together, they invite us to consider who gets to occupy, shape and reclaim our cities, and how diverse lives, livelihoods and aspirations can coexist within them.

This event is in conjunction with programming for Beneath the Turning Sky.

name: Neural Naatak: A Techno-Magic Performance
description:
Neural Natak is a speculative fiction performance by Mumbai-based artist Spryk that imagines neural networks as practitioners of technomagic—an ancient-future craft where technology and illusion merge. The performance fuses cutting-edge Gen-AI visuals & electronic music, inspired by Indian street magic & ritual theatre, into a mixed-media performance, exploring how archival intelligence remembers these rarely documented yet rich subcultures from India’s past. The soundtrack for Neural Natak features electronic music production informed by more traditional musical structures, creating a grand soundstage. The score is interwoven with folk percussion-inspired layered rhythms accentuated with razor-sharp textures.

This event is part of Art is Life: Elsewhere  hosted in collaboration with Goethe Institut/Max Mueller Bhavan, as an offshoot series of programs as part of our annual festival Art is Life.

name: From Stone to Story: Odissi through Sculpture
description:
Explore the relationship between visual art and movement in this immersive Odissi workshop. Beginning with a sculpture, participants will discover how Odisha’s artistic traditions have shaped the classical dance form, exploring its vocabulary through body awareness, Chauka, Tribhangi, mudras, rhythm and abhinaya.

Through demonstrations, discussions and hands-on exercises, participants will experiment with translating visual forms into movement and storytelling. The session will culminate in a collaborative movement composition, followed by learning a simple Odissi phrase and reflecting on the artwork that inspired the experience.

This workshop is part of the ongoing series, Responding to Art through the Arts. Facilitated by arts practitioners, it aims to activate MAP’s galleries through a series of workshops that hold space for young people’s responses to artwork on display. 

It is conducted as part of our engagements for the MAP Youth Collective – a community for young people (18-25 year olds) to engage with the arts and culture sector. The collective is for, of and by young people — to explore our shared identities and interests through art
